objectives: State the reactants and products of photosynthesis.
Recall photosynthesis is endothermic and write the equations.
Describe the uses of the glucose a plant makes.
Explain how light, carbon dioxide and temperature change the rate (limiting factors).
Interpret a rate graph and describe the required practical with pondweed.

keyVocabulary.meaning: how a plant makes its own food (glucose) using light energy
what you start with: carbon dioxide and water
what is made: glucose and oxygen
a reaction that takes IN energy from the surroundings
the green pigment that absorbs (traps) light energy
the part of a plant cell where photosynthesis happens
the thing in shortest supply that slows the rate down
how fast the reaction happens (e.g. bubbles per minute)

explain: Plants cannot move to find food, so they make their own using light energy from the Sun. Photosynthesis is endothermic, which means it takes in energy.
Light energy is trapped by chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts. The energy joins carbon dioxide (from the air) and water (from the soil) together.
This makes glucose, a sugar the plant uses for energy and growth. Oxygen is made as well and is released into the air.
wordEquation: carbon dioxide + water  →(light + chlorophyll)→  glucose + oxygen
glucoseUses: Used in respiration to release energy.
Used to make cellulose for strong cell walls.
Used (with nitrate ions) to make amino acids for proteins.
limitingFactors: Light intensity — more light means a faster rate, until something else runs short.
Carbon dioxide concentration — more CO₂ means a faster rate, up to a point.
Temperature — warmth speeds it up, but too hot damages the enzymes and it slows down.
Amount of chlorophyll — less chlorophyll (e.g. diseased leaves) means a slower rate.

content.title: Remember (content)
lines: IN (reactants): carbon dioxide + water.   OUT (products): glucose + oxygen.
Where: chloroplasts in the leaf.   Energy: light, trapped by chlorophyll.
Photosynthesis is endothermic (takes IN energy). Plants also respire — day and night.

method.title: How to answer an 'explain' question
lines: 2  Say WHY, using a key word (light / chlorophyll / chloroplast / limiting factor).
3  Link back to the question (so... / this means...).
Example: 'There is no light, so chlorophyll cannot trap energy, so no glucose is made.'

commonMistakes: Swapping the gases. The plant takes IN carbon dioxide and gives OUT oxygen — for example, the bubbles from pondweed are oxygen.
Calling light a raw material. The raw materials (reactants) are water and carbon dioxide; light is the energy source.
Saying it happens 'in the leaf'. Be exact: it happens in the chloroplast inside the leaf cell.
Forgetting plants respire too. Plants photosynthesise AND respire — respiration never stops, day or night.
Writing the equation backwards. Reactants (CO₂ + water) go on the LEFT; products (glucose + oxygen) on the RIGHT.

questions.prompt: State the two reactants (raw materials) needed for photosynthesis.
Name the two products made in photosynthesis.
Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

questions.hint: Think about energy — is it taken in or given out?

questions.prompt:
Look at the diagram below.
(a) Name structure A.
(b) Name the green pigment that structure A contains.
Give three different ways a plant uses the glucose it makes.

Look at the graph below.
(a) Describe what happens to the rate of photosynthesis as light intensity increases.

questions.frame:
(a) As light intensity increases, the rate ____.
(b) The rate levels off because ____ is now the limiting factor.
questions.hint: When light is no longer in short supply, another factor (carbon dioxide or temperature) becomes the limiting factor.

questions.prompt:
A student investigates the effect of light intensity on photosynthesis. They move a lamp closer to pondweed and count the gas bubbles each minute (see diagram).
(a) Name the gas in the bubbles.
(b) Give one variable they must keep the same (control).
(c) State one way they could make the results more accurate.
questions.hint: Control variables here include temperature and the amount of carbon dioxide. For accuracy, repeat and find a mean.

questions.prompt: A farmer grows tomatoes in a greenhouse during winter. The tomatoes are growing slowly. Explain how the farmer could increase the rate of photosynthesis so the tomatoes grow faster. In your answer, refer to more than one limiting factor.
questions.frame:
One way is to ____ because ____.
Another way is to ____ because ____.
The farmer must also think about ____ (e.g. cost).
questions.hint: Use the three limiting factors: light, carbon dioxide and temperature. Say WHAT to change and WHY it speeds up the rate.

answers.title: Teacher answer key
rows: Q3: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light + chlorophyll above the arrow).
Q4: It takes in energy from the surroundings (here, light energy).
Q6: Any three of: respiration (energy); growth; stored as starch; making cellulose for cell walls; making amino acids/proteins (with nitrate ions).

Q7: (a) The rate increases as light intensity increases. (b) It levels off because another factor (carbon dioxide concentration or temperature) becomes the limiting factor — light is no longer limiting.
Q8: (a) Oxygen. (b) Any one: temperature / amount of carbon dioxide / same piece of pondweed. (c) Repeat and calculate a mean (or count for a fixed time).

Q9 (6 marks, indicative): Increase light (lamps) — gives more energy for the reaction; add carbon dioxide (e.g. CO₂ burner) — more raw material; raise the temperature (heater) — enzymes work faster (but not too hot or enzymes denature). Must reference more than one factor and link change → faster rate; may mention balancing cost.
